extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers and journalists interested in race, performance, and cultural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive, encyclopedic overview of blackface use, controversies, and cultural contexts worldwide, focusing on performance, media, tradition, and public response. The page presents examples, debates about representation, and editorial/cultural reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackface solidifies stereotypes regardless of intent
rubrics_metrics.description: “the use of black-face solidifies stereotypes regardless of any good intentions and supports racist structures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raised by protesters of Deutsches Theater productions (e.g., Unschuld); prompted discussion between critics and theatre directors and led to changes in actor make-up and public reflection. Used as an evaluative principle to judge performances that employ racialized make-up even if intended as critique or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic casting and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics noted that white actors being cast in black roles can reveal a systemic problem: “white actors are accounted to be qualified for all roles, even black ones, while black actors are suitable only for black roles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate production practices and hiring policies; examples include debates around German productions of I'm Not Rappaport and Clybourne Park, and calls to cast black actors in black roles rather than using make-up or race-swapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of historic works
rubrics_metrics.description: Older films and performances should be evaluated in the context of their own time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulated by Yle in relation to a 1960 film; guidance informs decisions whether to air, edit, or provide contextual framing for archival material—some broadcasters leave content unaired while others present it with commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid racialising negative traits when depicting characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising and comedy that portray negative traits (e.g., corruption, dishonesty) should not racialise the character: complaint stated the commercial was offensive as it portrays a stereotype that black politicians are liars and that “there was no need for the man to be made out to be black.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by regulators and standards bodies (e.g., Advertising Standards Authority of South Africa) to assess commercials and sketches; led to pulling or halting of ads and public complaints (examples: Vodacom ad, Leon Schuster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackface is inherently racist (as a standard of offense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory or complaint language describing blackface as “an inherently racist form of acting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoked in formal complaints and by anti-racist groups to justify halting broadcasts, removing content, or disciplining performers; shapes policy decisions by broadcasters and advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/traditional uses may be framed as celebration or remembrance
rubrics_metrics.description: In some traditions blackface is used as a form of celebration of African history or as an emancipatory symbol (e.g., Portobelo's Carnival in Panama), serving functions such as remembering ancestors, disguising fugitives, or signalling community codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers an explanatory rubric for why some communities continue blackening faces as heritage practice; used to weigh cultural continuity and local meaning against wider critiques of racial caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast and editorial response to public criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters and networks may edit, remove, or refuse to air blackface segments after public outcry or internal review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fuji TV edited a blackface segment after review; Netflix pulled an episode that featured blackface; CCTV segments provoked editing and debate. Guidance used by media organizations when deciding how to handle contested content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggerated caricature features (e.g., bright red lips, exaggerated features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical portrayals often employed exaggerated features (bright red lips, oversized features) that are now identified as harmful caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples include Soviet-era illustrations, Dakkochan toys, Mr. Popo and Jynx controversies; used to judge visual depictions and to justify censorship, redesign, or contextualisation of characters and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackface as cultural appropriation and exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackface is seen as ‘epitomizing an appropriation and imitation of black culture’ and as part of a continuum that profits from and exploits black artistic contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in legacy analyses tracing how black performance styles were adopted and monetised by white performers; used as a criterion to critique cultural borrowing, power imbalances, and commercial appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public protest and activism can prompt institutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Public protests, petitions and activism over blackface performances or traditions can lead to alterations in productions, cancellations, or changes in institutional practice (e.g., make-up redesigns, cancelled productions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented instances: Deutsches Theater make-up change after protest; cancellation or rescheduling of productions (e.g., SLĀV, Kanata controversies); Joint Morris Organisation moving to eliminate full-face black makeup. Used as a measure of accountability and decision-making pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some communities or performers defend blackface as harmless or traditional
rubrics_metrics.description: In some contexts there remains a belief that blackface is harmless fun or a cherished tradition (e.g., certain Mexican cartoons, some South African carnival minstrels), creating contested interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stance factors into debates and policy decisions and explains why change can be uneven: examples include political support for Memín Pinguín in Mexico and differing public reactions in China and parts of Latin America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical practical rationale: lack of access to black performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, theatres and film industries sometimes used blackface because they rarely had access to black actors, leading to darkening of skin for roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical practices in Soviet theatre and early ballets (e.g., Petrushka, the Moor in Sheherazade); used to contextualise but not excuse continued use, and to inform modern choices about casting and historical staging.
